name: regex-lite (small, fast-building regex)
baseline: regex 1.9.0 with every feature disabled except std (build time and binary size); regex 1.12.2 for regex compile and search time
verdict_reason: The author's experiment shows regex-lite building in 0.73s against 1.93s and adding 94KB against 565KB, and rebar ranks it far ahead on Regex::new time (2.73 vs 11.85). Those are the claims it makes; it does not claim faster searches, and rebar shows it is much slower there (search geometric mean 156.49 vs 3.08).
tier_reason: First-party numbers: one build experiment with no machine or rustc stated, plus the author's own rebar runs without hardware details.
claimed_speedup: Build: 0.73s vs 1.93s compile time and 94KB vs 565KB relative size increase (regex-lite 0.1.0 vs regex 1.9.0 with only std); Regex::new: compile-time geometric mean 2.73 vs 11.85 in rebar (lower is better). Search is slower: geometric mean 156.49 vs 3.08; literal sherlock-en 74.4 MB/s vs 29.4 GB/s.
workload: Compile time and binary-size increase of a program depending on the crate; rebar compile-time and search-time benchmarks (10 and 28 benchmarks for regex-lite).
one_liner: Drop-in subset of the regex crate that builds in about 40% of the time and adds about a sixth of the binary size, at the cost of much slower searches.
how_it_is_fast: It skips the meta engine, DFAs, literal prefilters and most Unicode tables and runs every search on a single PikeVM, so there is much less code to compile and link. Less analysis at Regex::new also makes pattern construction faster. It keeps the linear-time search guarantee.
use_it_when: CLI tools, build scripts or WASM bundles where binary size and compile time matter more than regex throughput
Programs that build many regexes and run each over short inputs
skip_it_when: Searching large haystacks: rebar's literal benchmark runs at 74.4 MB/s vs 29.4 GB/s for regex
Patterns that need Unicode classes or Unicode case folding, which regex-lite leaves out
caveats: The build-time numbers come from one experiment on an unstated machine
The rebar summary ranks each engine over the benchmarks it can run, and regex-lite skips the Unicode-heavy ones
tradeoffs: Search throughput is one to three orders of magnitude lower than regex on literal-heavy workloads

evidence.quote: For `regex`, I disabled all features except for `std`:
| rust/regex | 29.4 GB/s | 10.5 GB/s | 35.6 GB/s | 8.4 GB/s | 47.7 GB/s |
